# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Despite major advances in guideline-directed medical therapy and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1]. CRT requires a prolonged QRS duration, leaving the majority of patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and a narrow QRS without an evidence-based device option [2]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) was developed to address this therapeutic gap. CCM delivers non-excitatory, high-voltage electrical impulses during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle, thereby enhancing myocardial contractility without increasing myocardial oxygen demand, and clinical studies have shown that CCM can improve exercise tolerance, quality of life, and left ventricular function.

## Mechanisms of Action

The biological rationale for CCM rests on preclinical work demonstrating that electrical stimulation during the refractory period augments contraction. Acute studies in dogs with experimentally induced HF showed that CCM signals applied to the failing myocardium during the absolute refractory period improved LV function without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption [3]. Foundational canine investigations established proof of concept [4], and subsequent work confirmed that CCM with non-excitatory electric signals improves left ventricular function in dogs with chronic heart failure [5], with sustained chronic benefit on function and remodeling [6]. Importantly, in patients, the enhanced inotropic state of the failing left ventricle by CCM electrical signals is not associated with increased myocardial oxygen consumption [7].

At the cellular level, the benefit arises from improved calcium cycling. Improved calcium handling (phosphorylation of phospholamban, upregulation of SERCA-2A), reversal of the fetal myocyte gene program associated with heart failure, and reverse remodeling are observed [8]. The central role of the SERCA2a/phospholamban axis in calcium homeostasis underpins these effects, since SR Ca-transport is mediated by SERCA2a and its regulatory phosphoprotein phospholamban; dephosphorylated phospholamban inhibits SERCA2a, and phosphorylation by protein kinases relieves this inhibition [9]. In human myocardium, CCM electrical signals induce reverse molecular remodeling, reversing the up-regulation of fetal and stretch-response genes and down-regulation of Ca²⁺ cycling genes characteristic of heart failure [10]. Normalization of the Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger has also been demonstrated [11]. A contemporary synthesis notes that these mechanisms might also serve to improve cardiovascular function for patients with higher ejection fractions, broadening the conceptual scope of therapy [12].

## Clinical Trial Evidence

The clinical program advanced through sequential trials. Lawo and colleagues reported on electrical signals applied during the absolute refractory period as an investigational treatment for advanced heart failure in patients with normal QRS duration [13], and a US feasibility study followed [14]. The first randomized study, FIX-HF-4, was a double-blind crossover trial: Borggrefe and colleagues performed a randomized, double-blind, crossover study of CCM signals in 164 subjects with ejection fraction below 35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms, showing improved peak VO₂ and quality of life [15].

The pivotal US FIX-HF-5 trial then enrolled a larger cohort. CCM was tested in 428 NYHA class III or IV, narrow-QRS HF patients with ejection fraction ≤35% randomized to optimal medical therapy plus CCM versus medical therapy alone [16]. That 428-patient study met its primary safety endpoint, a noninferiority assessment of the composite of all-cause mortality and all-cause hospitalizations, though the primary efficacy endpoint was not met overall [17]. A prespecified subgroup analysis identified greater benefit in patients with ejection fraction ≥25% [18], and the design rationale for a confirmatory trial was published [19].

The confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial validated these findings. A total of 160 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration <130 ms, and ejection fraction between 25% and 45% were randomized to medical therapy or CCM for 24 weeks, and the difference in peak VO₂ between groups satisfied the primary endpoint [20]. A two-lead system was subsequently evaluated in FIX-HF-5C2: the change in peak VO₂ was 1.72 mL/kg per minute greater in the 2-lead device group versus controls, and 83.1% of subjects experienced at least one NYHA class improvement [21]. These data supported FDA approval of the Optimizer Smart System in 2019 [22].

Pooled analyses reinforce the functional benefit. An individual patient data meta-analysis of randomized trials suggests that CCM has significant if somewhat modest benefits in improving measures of functional capacity and quality of life [23], and a comprehensive 2020 individual patient data meta-analysis confirmed benefits across functional capacity and HF-related quality of life [24].

## Real-World and Emerging Data

Registry data extend these observations to clinical practice. CCM-REG, a prospective registry of 503 patients from 51 European centres, found that CCM improved functional status, quality of life and LVEF, reduced heart failure hospitalization rates, and was associated with survival at 1 and 3 years significantly better than predicted by the MAGGIC risk score [25]. Single-centre long-term experience reported favorable survival and efficacy [26], and case-control data have suggested a long-term survival benefit [27]. Interest is growing in patients with higher ejection fractions; a pilot study (CCM-HFpEF) reported improved health status in HF with preserved ejection fraction [28], reflecting the mechanistic hypothesis that benefit may extend across the EF spectrum [12].

## Guidelines and Future Directions

CCM is incorporated into contemporary practice. The 2016 ESC HF guidelines and the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline, which replaced prior documents, provide patient-centric recommendations for managing heart failure, addressing device-based therapies including CCM [29, 30]. Ongoing development of integrated CCM-defibrillator platforms and simplified lead configurations may further broaden applicability [6]. Nonetheless, large randomized trials powered for hard clinical endpoints remain limited, and prospective outcome data are needed to define the precise role of CCM in HF care pathways.
